content:
Hello, I am a student at Imperial College London, working on my master's thesis involving formalisation of the Lilac Probabilistic Separation Logic. (I have asked some questions on this channel before). There has been quite some progress on formalising the soundness of the system (repo here), but I am skipping ahead to the integration with Iris, which I am most anxious about. For the purpose of this question, the only thing to note about Lilac is that it is first order, hence I am only instantiating MoSeL, the frontend of Iris (step indexing, OFE, etc are not relevant to my project). I have been trying to understand how the proofmode works, and I am interested in contributing upstream to Iris-lean (intro_patterns issue lists a few things I could work on for eg.). Here are my questions:

  1. Just to confirm, the iintro(s) tactic is intended to work on both implications and forall quantifiers, right?
  2. In my program logic, I define LProp (lilac prop) like so:
abbrev LProp (rs : List TyRand) := {sem : Env rs → Resource → Prop // ∀ s σ₁ σ₂, σ₁ ≤ σ₂ → sem s σ₁ → sem s σ₂}

What I like to point out here is that I have used Dependent De Brujin Indices, so my "variable store" (called Env above), takes a parameter rs constraining the number and (Lilac) types of the values in the store.

This causes trouble with the instantiation of sForall in BI. sForall : (LProp rs → Prop) → LProp (r :: rs)
is not possible (I am adding an additional variable of type r to the environment). So I can't instantiate sForall.

Has this been tried before? Is it a standard solution not to use Dependent De Brujin, and instead have a mapping along with a well-formedness predicate? How do fresh unique ID's get generated for new variables, in this approach?

  1. I have slightly simplified my requirements in the above description. I actually have two types of variables (deterministic and random, details not important), and the Env ds rs is a tuple of EnvDet ds and EnvRand rs. The two types of variables are treated separately, so there are actually two forall quantifiers. I have defined forall_det and forall_rand and logic specific connectives separate to sForall from BIBase thereby temporarily circumventing the problem from point 2. This leads me in the direction of developing custom iintro tactic for my custom forall quantifiers. Does this sound like a good idea. Is it likely that I will still be able to use all the rest of the tactics provided by the Iris proofmode, smoothly? Or does using a non-standard forall mean I am no longer compatible with the rest of the framework immediately?

I can't quite answer the above question myself, or tell is if it is a reasonable question, as I am unfamiliar with the internals of the proofmode (though I would like to learn more about it and contribute to it).

Any suggestions, advice, feedback and partial answers is much appreciated. I would particularly like to know if I am going down a direction which is known not to work/cause problems.

Hi Edwin, it is great that you are reaching out about this! I don't fully understand what you are trying to do, but I will try to answer as best as I can, but others can also chime in.

Just to confirm, the iintro(s) tactic is intended to work on both implications and forall quantifiers, right?

Yes. See for example here.

Has this been tried before? Is it a standard solution not to use Dependent De Brujin, and instead have a mapping along with a well-formedness predicate? How do fresh unique ID's get generated for new variables, in this approach?

Not sure if this has been tried before. Usually, Iris-based projects use a less fancy system for variables than Dependent De Brujin. E.g. HeapLang just uses strings without any well-formedness predicates. There was actually a recent discussion about generating fresh variables in HeapLang recently on the Iris Helpdesk. But my understanding is that most of the time Iris is used to verify concrete programs and there all variables are already there and do not need to be generated freshly, so maybe this problem does not show up.

Is it likely that I will still be able to use all the rest of the tactics provided by the Iris proofmode, smoothly? Or does using a non-standard forall mean I am no longer compatible with the rest of the framework immediately?

The key questions is whether you can implement the BI interface or not. If you can implement the BI interface with whatever definition of ∀ that satisfies the requirements of the interface, you can use the proofmode for your logic. If you have custom connectives like you custom forall, you can then add support for them in the proof mode by implementing the right typeclasses, like FromForall and IntoForall. If you implement these typeclasses for your custom forall, you will be able to use iintro for it.

I hope this helps. Let me know if you have any further questions.

Thank you for the very helpful answer. FromForall and IntoForall was the missing link, and I am now able to introduce variables! I have to think more about if the Dependent De Brujin indices are required, but atleast for now its not a problem.

Hello again, I am still very confused on how to deal with variable binders and substitutions. Particularly, how the language and logic talk can somehow talk about the same variables (my current approach uses substitution functions, which object logic can't reduce and only the meta logic can. So I get stuck if trying to proceed in the Iris proofmode). I believe the string-based approach might not work well in my context. The problem is that the semantics of my object language is given as a bundled function (function + prop) from the environment to some objectLang value of objectLang type. And the domain of this function is a list of values (I call Env) and not a bunch of strings.

  1. Does IrisLean Heaplang use a different approach. Since it uses metaprogramming, is it correct that it uses Lean's inbuilt binder management discipline. I was wondering if I should try to use this metaprogramming/embedded dsl approach.
  2. I want some practice with metaprogramming and understand of Iris proofmode. Would you recommend this issue https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/issues/213 (if so) a particular tactic within it to start with?

I have to admit I still don't fully understand how exactly the binders in your language work, so I am not sure what exactly your problem is. But it seems like the problem can maybe be phrased as an Iris question instead of just an Iris Lean question. In this case, I would recommend that you ask at the Iris Helpdesk. There are more people there who have maybe tried to do something similar to what you are trying to do.

About your questions:

Edwin Fernando said:

  1. Does IrisLean Heaplang use a different approach. Since it uses metaprogramming, is it correct that it uses Lean's inbuilt binder management discipline.

No, IrisLean Heplang does not use Lean's inbuilt binder management discipline. It just uses strings for binders (like in Rocq). See here, variables are simply strings.

Edwin Fernando said:

  1. Would you recommend this issue https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/issues/213 (if so) a particular tactic within it to start with?

I would recommend to look at https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/issues/239 for an overview of the missing tactics. If you want a (hopefully) simple tactic to implement I would recommend to look at iAccu. If you decide to work on this, please comment on the corresponding issues (https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/issues/364) to make sure that there is no duplicate work.

Edwin Fernando said:

Hello, I am a student at Imperial College London, working on my master's thesis involving formalisation of the Lilac Probabilistic Separation Logic.

This seems very exciting! We are also formalizing Bluebell on top of iris-lean: https://github.com/Verified-zkEVM/iris-lean. Perhaps our formalization has dealt with these issues (though I'm not the main person, probably @Julian Sutherland is more qualified to answer)

Quang Dao said:

This seems very exciting! We are also formalizing Bluebell on top of iris-lean: https://github.com/Verified-zkEVM/iris-lean.

Very cool! Slightly diverging from the original topic, but is there a reason why you are using a fork of Iris Lean instead of depending on it as a library?

Michael Sammler said:

I have to admit I still don't fully understand how exactly the binders in your language work, so I am not sure what exactly your problem is.

Sorry I didn't really try to explain that. Maybe I shouldn't use the word 'binders'. I was just referring to my use of dependent de brujin indices vs the standard string-based method.

Quang Dao said:

This seems very exciting! We are also formalizing Bluebell on top of iris-lean: https://github.com/Verified-zkEVM/iris-lean. Perhaps our formalization has dealt with these issues (though I'm not the main person, probably Julian Sutherland is more qualified to answer)

I am aware of this! Bluebell has a different approach to variables where the variables are part of the resource unlike Lilac. My understanding is that this is a difference due to Bluebell being a logic for an imperative language vs Lilac for a functional language. So Bluebell doesn't have the problem I am facing (is my guess).

I have since thought more about my problem. And I think my question about variables was ill-posed. The problem isn't really about whether I use Dependent de Brujin Indices or a string-based representation. The problem arises from variables have a different Lean type in language vs in the logic. In the logic a variable is of type A, while in language, the same variable has type RV A which is an alias for {f : B -> A // Measurable f}. Essentially in the logic the variable has a related but different type. This is certainly a plain Iris question not an Iris lean question, so I will ask it in the Iris Helpdesk, after thinking about it more. Thank you for the suggestion Michael.
